queue.title: Survey Sunday: When self driving cars crash, who gets the blame?
queue.text:
For the last few weeks, we’ve been running a sidebar survey about whether our
Electrek
readers who should be held responsible when AI fails, and people get hurt. After nearly 3,000 responses, here’s what you told us.

In case you missed the survey, the question read, “
A number of fatal Tesla accidents
are making headlines
while Waymo racks up thousands of parking tickets
, and the sheer volume of autonomous taxis means those numbers will keep climbing – but when an AI-driven taxi fails, who should be responsible?”

The survey coincided with both the re-unveiling of the Tesla Cybercab earlier this month in Austin
, Texas,
and news that the long-delayed Tesla Semi had begun series production in Nevada
. As such, it shouldn’t be surprising that there were a lot of responses. What was surprising (to me, at least), was just how many people were ready to absolve the person behind the steering wheel of any wrongdoing when things went sideways.

Just 102 votes (about 3.5%) were cast for the personal responsibility option that read, “Whoever is sitting in the driver’s seat: even if YOU summoned the taxi, it’s common sense that human intervention will sometimes be required, and YOU are the human.” And, for what it’s worth, at
least
two of those votes were from me (sue me).

This one seemed genuinely obvious to me, but that’s what interacting with the other humans is all about: listening, learning, and growing. And what I heard, learned, and grew to finally believe, myself, is that it was the owner of the vehicle who should shoulder the burden of liability – that belief was fueled by commenters like Ian …

This is obvious. Whether the driver is AI or the human, the liable person is the owner of the car. If I lend my car to you and you drive it into a coffee shop, I get to pay for the damages. The car is insured, not the driver. I don’t know why people are asking this question. It is well settled in existing law.

IAN

… and pushedbyvolts, who (I thought) said it best …

Whoever owns the vehicle should get the blame. Every car ever built is capable of breaking the law and the driver gets the blame when it happens. If there’s no driver, the registered owner is the responsible party for putting a lawbreaking vehicle on the street. If that screws up someone’s driverless taxi business model, so be it.

PUSHEDBYVOLTS

… by pointing out the fact that, yes, every car ever built actually is capable of breaking the law – whether that’s by speeding, parking illegally, or being intentionally used as a weapon against another person. And, in every one of those cases, it seems insane to even consider holding a manufacturer or a technology supplier liable.

That said, nearly 90% of the votes put the blame squarely on the developers of the AI driving the car. Stephen Fields’ comment made, I think, the most compelling case for this:

What action could the owner have taken to prevent an accident? They buy a black box which drives the vehicle. If the owner failed to follow the recommendations of the manufacturer (ie keep software up to date, stay in this geofence) they could be liable but they could not be held liable if there is no action they could have taken to prevent an accident.

[IMG:1]

STEPHEN FIELDS

That argument also makes a ton of sense, though I would argue that summoning a vehicle that offered you no means of saving yourself when other options were readily available is, in itself, an assumption of liability – but when other options aren’t available? That’s a different story, and there’s a bunch of nuance to parse through that lays blame at the feet of both the manufacturer and the AI developer, to varying degrees.

No matter who eventually gets the blame, however, regular commenter BCGeiger delivered what I considered to be the coup de grâce in this case:

I think liability should be split evenly between the car manufacturer and the AI manufacturer. It isn’t (an) either or thing. They are working hand-in-hand to bring about this hellscape.

BCGEIGER

For me there is an easy test: if you take away the AI driving, would the accident have happened?

In other words, a normal car: driver is at fault. If you loan your car to a buddy and her runs over a pedestrian, he's going to jail, not you.

AI driver is always going to be at fault.

Even if an Auto Pilot type of system simply causes mode confusion in the human driver, and the human does not intervene, I still think that lands squarely on the AI mfg, for setting up a situation that mode confusion can happen.

No AI driver, no mode confusion.

I'm an engineer, and spend about 10% of my time designing and about 90% checking all the ways the design could fail (technically still "designing") including checking for forseeable mis-use. That's what keeps me up at night. Predicting all the ways people will mis-understand the design intent is the hardest part (unknown unknowns, can't prove a negative, etc).

“Hellscape” is what sold it for me, but then I just turned around and asked a different AI to make the featured image (at top) and to help me pretty up the graph, above, so what do I know? Let us know if you agree with the nearly 9/10
Electrekkers
who responded to the original survey, or if we all got it wrong, in the comments.

Original content from
Electrek
.

queue.title: NIO sells 30% of battery swap unit to Geely at more than $2 billion
queue.text:
Geely is buying into NIO’s battery swap network. NIO announced definitive agreements on Sunday that hand a Geely Holding subsidiary 30% of NIO Power, the unit running its swap stations and chargers, at a post-money valuation of about RMB16 billion ($2.4 billion).

Most of what Geely is paying isn’t cash. It’s contributing its own commercial battery swap business plus RMB640 million ($94 million), while NIO takes 10% of Geely’s charging arm in a parallel deal.

Here’s how the NIO Power side breaks down,
according to NIO’s announcement
:

At the deal valuation, a 30% stake is worth about RMB4.8 billion. Take out the cash, and NIO is effectively valuing Yiyi at a little over RMB4.1 billion ($610 million). That’s what the milestone clause is for. If Yiyi’s business doesn’t deliver, Geely ends up with less of NIO Power.

The second leg runs the other way. NIO China is subscribing to newly issued shares of Zhejiang Haohan Energy Technology, Geely’s charging business, for a 10% stake. Haohan will then use that cash to buy some of NIO’s charging assets. NIO didn’t disclose the amount, but in practice it’s trading part of its charging network for equity in Geely’s.

Both transactions still need regulatory approval.

NIO has been pitching its swap network to other automakers for years. Back in 2021, it
announced plans to open its battery swap stations to other automakers
, and we asked at the time if anyone would bite. Geely signed a strategic partnership on swapping with NIO in November 2023, promising joint standards for private and commercial vehicles. But that was a handshake. This one comes with assets and cash.

The network is big. NIO had 3,790 swap stations when it passed 100 million swaps in February, and it’s targeting 1,000 more this year. It also
set a record of 175,976 swaps in a single day
earlier this year. Swapping is also what makes NIO’s Battery-as-a-Service pricing possible, which it used to bring the
ES9 flagship SUV in at $54K
.

But it’s expensive to build, and NIO has spent a long time looking for someone to help carry it. NIO Power’s first outside money came in May 2024: RMB1.5 billion led by the same Wuhan Guangchuang fund that will hold 6.4% after this deal. Then in March 2025, NIO said CATL was “advancing an investment capped at RMB 2.5 billion” in NIO Power. CATL isn’t in the ownership table NIO published today.

[IMG:1]

The valuation hasn’t moved much either. The Wuhan fund’s 6.4% works out to about 9.1% before Geely comes in. If nothing else changed in the cap table, that puts NIO Power at roughly RMB16 billion back in 2024, when the network had far fewer stations than it does now.

NIO isn’t selling from a position of desperation, though. It delivered 107,658 vehicles in Q2 2026, posted an 18.5% vehicle margin, and eked out a small non-GAAP profit,
according to its latest earnings
. It still lost RMB528 million on a GAAP basis, and it had RMB56.7 billion in cash at the end of June.

Geely Holding is the parent of Geely Auto, Zeekr, Lynk & Co, Volvo Cars, and Polestar. Yiyi, the business it’s folding into NIO Power, focuses on commercial swapping for fleets rather than private cars.

According to NIO, the two companies have “preliminary plans” to bring battery swapping to consumer models from Geely-related entities, as well as to its commercial mobility businesses. Those plans still need to be finalized.

That’s the part that matters. China’s swap market is splitting into camps: NIO’s network, CATL’s Choco-Swap network, and BYD betting on ultra-fast charging instead. A Geely brand shipping NIO-compatible packs at volume would make NIO’s network the default for a huge chunk of the market.

queue.title: Full Self Hauling: Volvo moves 3 million tonnes of Earth, autonomously
queue.text:
The deployed fleet of ultra heavy-duty trucks and mining equipment assets powered by Volvo Autonomous Solutions reached a major milestone last week, hauling their 3
millionth
tonne of material out of the mines without a human driver.

Volvo CE
deployed its first pilot-ready autonomous hauling solutions with customers Boliden Garpenberg in Sweden and Brønnøy Kalk in Norway back 2023, with a milestone of 1 moving million tonnes (~1.1 US tons) of Earth autonomously by 2025.

Sharp readers will note that it is now 2026, and Volvo has blown past the original pilot’s goal, crossing the three million ton mark at Boliden’s Garpenberg mine earlier this summer. Volvo Autonomous Solutions (VAS)
announced the achievement last week with a press release and a bunch of great new equipment photos
– and Volvo executives, to their credit, seem super-hyped about the progress being made there.

“Reaching three million tonnes hauled autonomously is an important milestone that demonstrates the maturity of our autonomous transport solution and the value it delivers in customer operations,” offers Ingo Stürmer, VAS’ CTO. “This achievement reflects years of close collaboration between the Volvo Autonomous Solutions team and our customers to develop, deploy,
and scale autonomous hauling in real-world environments
.”

Volvo calls its autonomous product line
, “Autona / earth,” and is marketing it as a, “complete solution for autonomous hauling, factory-assembled,” by bundling the trucks, software, physical on-site infrastructure, and operational support into a single service in a bid to make autonomous hauling solutions easier for mines and quarries to deploy without the need to become autonomy experts themselves.

[IMG:1]

Projects like this,
and the autonomous Huawei-automated coal mine in Mongolia we covered back in March
, are part of a larger shift taking place across the global mining sector. While passenger EV adoption dominates the headlines, the strongest economic arguments for electrification are often in industrial and logistical applications where vehicles follow fixed routes, consume enormous amounts of energy, and operate around the clock.

In those environments, every gallon of diesel displaced translates directly into measurable savings –
more than enough savings
, in many cases, to justify either a massive self-driving tech spend or a few hundred dollars’ worth of top-shelf LEGO sets to put in your office. You can check those out, below, then let us know what you think of Volvo’s mining milestone in the comments.

queue.title: Tesla warns weather could delay Roadster demo, and the forecast is ugly
queue.text:
Update 9/28:
Tesla has since confirmed that it’s rescheduling the Roadster event to October 15, citing “severe conditions predicted.”
We have more on the two-week delay here
.

Tesla is warning guests invited to its October 1 Roadster event that the long-delayed demo could get pushed back again, and this time it’s the weather.

In an email to invitees, Tesla says the event “must be held outdoors” and may need to be rescheduled. And the forecast for central Texas on Thursday calls for an 82% chance of rain, with thunderstorms.

The email, titled “Important: Roadster Event Weather,” was shared by one of the invitees. Tesla tells the guest it’s “looking forward to hosting you” on October 1, 2026, then adds that “there is a possibility we may need to reschedule due to weather.”

According to Tesla, the event “features a unique experience that must be held outdoors,” and the company is “continuing to monitor weather reports.” There’s no backup date in the email, only a promise to “reach out with additional details as soon as possible.”

Tesla
teased the October 1 reveal earlier this month
with a “Go for launch” image. As we
reported in August
, the centerpiece is a hover demonstration using a SpaceX-developed cold gas thruster package, code-named A71, at SpaceX’s rocket test site in McGregor, Texas, just outside Waco. The car is expected to run remotely with nobody inside, and spectators are to be kept several hundred yards back because the thrusters are loud enough to damage eardrums.

So “outdoors” isn’t a stylistic choice. You don’t fire thrusters in a tent.

Open-Meteo forecast data for McGregor, pulled Monday morning, shows an 82% chance of precipitation on Thursday, October 1, with thunderstorms in the forecast and wind gusts up to 32 mph.

Friday isn’t much better on rain at 75%, but the wind drops to gusts around 13 mph. By Saturday, the chance of rain falls to 42%.

Forecasts three days out can still move. But thunderstorms and 30+ mph gusts are about the last conditions you’d pick for making a car hover on cold gas thrusters in front of a crowd.

[IMG:1]

Tesla unveiled the next-gen Roadster prototype in November 2017 and promised production in 2020. The timeline has slipped at least eight times since.

The demo alone has moved repeatedly. Musk
said last October
a “flying” demo was coming by the end of 2025. A week later,
Tesla pushed it to April 1, 2026, and production to 2027 or 2028
. April became “maybe in a month or so” on the Q1 earnings call, then
August
, then October 1.

Reservation holders put down $50,000 for a standard Roadster and $250,000 for the Founders Series. Nearly nine years later, nobody has a car.

In a related story, the Elon forecast is calling for a 100% chance of stock pumping, a 95% chance of further timeline slippage, and a 90% chance of lies relating to price and performance.

While this would be delay number 12 after 9 years, at least this one isn’t on Musk. Tesla can’t control thunderstorms in Texas, and if the forecast holds, postponing a remote-controlled hover stunt with a crowd nearby is the responsible call.

But it tells you a lot about the Roadster program that the biggest risk to its launch event is wind and rain. A car you can actually buy and drive doesn’t need clear skies to be shown off. A stunt with SpaceX hardware does.

If Tesla does have to push it, we expect days, not months. The real question is what shows up when it finally happens: a production-intent car with final specs, a price, and a delivery date, or another flashy video that resets the clock?

queue.title: Volkswagen’s best-seller is going electric in 2027 to replace the ID.4 and ID.5 [Images]
queue.text:
Volkswagen is taking its best-seller electric. The ID. Tiguan will replace
the ID.4
and ID.5 as part of Volkswagen’s revamped lineup in 2027.

With more than 950,000 models sold since they went on sale in 2021, the ID.4 and ID.5 have been among Volkswagen’s best-selling electric vehicles.

As part of Volkswagen’s revamped lineup, the ID.4 and ID.5 are next in line for an overhaul that brings more than just a new name.

Following the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, the ID. Tiguan will go on sale in 2027 as a “True Volkswagen,” bringing a new look, updated tech, and a refined interior.

“The all-electric model builds on the strengths of the bestseller and offers premium design, generous space, intuitive operation, and innovative technologies,” Volkswagen Brand CEO Thomas Shafer said.

In the past year, Volkswagen delivered over 1 million Tiguan and Tayron models globally. Both are available in petrol, diesel, and plug-in hybrid (PHEV), so adding an all-electric option makes sense.

The ID. Tiguan will go on sale in early 2027, starting in Europe, replacing the ID.4 and ID.5 in Volkswagen’s lineup. The US and other global markets will follow shortly after.

Volkswagen released several images of a camouflaged ID. Tiguan prototype, offering a sneak peek at the new look.

Although it’s still covered, the new images confirm the changes we’ve seen in
recent spy images
. The ID. Tiguan will adopt a boxier, more traditional SUV-like design that’s nearly identical to the gas-powered version.

[IMG:1]

You can see the prototype has pop-out door handles, replacing the flush style used on the ID.4 and ID.5.

"The ID. Tiguan will adopt a boxier, more traditional SUV-like design that’s nearly identical to the gas-powered version."

This is exactly what would keep me from going into this vs the ID.4 like I had. Since I don't really like SUV's and hate the looks of most of them, but also since getting a sedan EV that fits into my budget is not really possible at this time, I have migrated to the ID.4 (2024) and now my 2026 Equinox EV. Both these vehicles look more wagon like than SUV, so that's good on my part. But this new ID.Tiguan is going all in on the SUV craze, and that turns me off. So for now I will continue with my Equinox wagon looking SUV until such time that I can buy a proper sedan EV. And since I recently picked up a clean 2017 Ford Focus EV sedan/hatch, I've been driving that more than my Equinox and will probably continue to until my daughter gets her DL. I purchased this Focus EV for her after all, but I love driving it. haha.

Volkswagen didn’t reveal any interior images, but the ID. Tiguan is expected to feature
Volkswagen’s new interior
design. Like the ID. Polo and ID. Cross (shown below), it will likely include VW’s new infotainment system, including the return of physical buttons.

We will have to wait until closer to launch for specifics, but with VW’s recent battery and drivetrain updates, the ID. Tiguan is expected to offer improved range, faster charging, and better cold-weather performance.

The current ID.4 uses an 82 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 291 miles in the RWD version. The AWD model offers around 263 miles. Under WLTP conditions, the 2026 VW ID.4 has a range of up to 351 miles (566 km).

Volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan will make its official debut in “early October,” but didn’t reveal a specific date. We should learn more soon. Check back for the latest.

queue.title: Omoda & Jaecoo confirm Canada launch in late 2026: here’s the EV lineup
queue.text:
Chery’s Omoda and Jaecoo brands have launched a Canadian website confirming that their “premium electric SUVs” will arrive in Canada in late 2026.

The site doesn’t name a single model, price, or dealer yet. But the Chinese automaker’s global lineup gives a pretty clear idea of what Canadians could get, and it’s heavy on plug-in hybrids.

A launch page with no cars on it

The new Omoda & Jaecoo Canada website is a teaser at this point. It tells visitors that “the wait is almost over” and that the brands are “coming late 2026,” with a sign-up form for updates.

[IMG:1]

The retailer locator is empty too. The company says it’s “building a network across Canada” and will announce locations ahead of the launch.

The site does include one telling bit of fine print: vehicles shown are intended for other markets, and some may not be available in Canada. In other words, Chery hasn’t picked its Canadian lineup yet, or at least isn’t saying.

On its “About” page, Omoda & Jaecoo claims it’s now sold in more than 75 countries and has exported over 1.2 million vehicles in about three years. The brand is growing fast in Europe. In the UK alone, it registered 6,238 vehicles in August for a 6.62% market share, according to the company.

[IMG:2]

Why now: Canada’s Chinese EV quota

This is a direct result of Canada slashing its 100% tariff on Chinese EVs to 6.1% back in January. The deal lets in up to 49,000 Chinese-made electrified vehicles per year at the lower rate, rising to 70,000 by 2030. Anything outside the quota still gets hit with the 100% surtax.

And for Chery, the quota covers plug-in hybrids and hybrids, not just battery-electric vehicles. That matters a lot given what Omoda and Jaecoo actually sell.

Chery has been preparing for a while. As we reported in May , it filed Canadian trademarks for Omoda, Jaecoo, and several other sub-brands, and Jaecoo E5 prototypes were spotted in Ontario on manufacturer plates.

[IMG:3]

It won’t be alone. BYD plans to open 20 Canadian dealerships in its first year, also targeting a late 2026 start. And Tesla is already using the quota to sell a Shanghai-built Model 3 at a record-low C$39,490 .

Omoda & Jaecoo’s current electrified lineup

We don’t know which of these will make it to Canada. Here’s what the brands currently offer in markets like the UK, Australia, and Indonesia, based on their official spec sheets.

The Jaecoo E5 is the most likely candidate to lead a Canadian launch, since it’s the one Chery was caught testing in Ontario. It’s a compact electric SUV with a 60.9 kWh battery, a 155 kW front motor, and 248 miles (399 km) of WLTP range. It does 0-100 km/h in 7.7 seconds.

[IMG:4]

It’s also cheap. The E5 starts at £27,505 in the UK and A$36,990 driveaway in Australia.

The catch is charging. Jaecoo UK lists an 80 kW DC peak, with 30-80% taking 27 minutes. That’s slow by 2026 standards.

The Omoda E5 is the sportier sibling on the same basic hardware: a 61 kWh battery, 155 kW motor, and 267 miles (430 km) of WLTP range. It charges from 30-80% in 28 minutes and starts at £33,065 in the UK.

The newest EV in the family launched in Indonesia in July. The Omoda 4 gets a bigger 65.05 kWh LFP pack, a 160 kW motor, 553 km of range on the optimistic NEDC cycle, and a 119 kW DC peak with 20-80% in 22 minutes. Pricing hasn’t been published yet.

[IMG:5]

This is the brand’s volume seller and it’s a plug-in hybrid. The Jaecoo 7 SHS-P pairs a 1.5-liter turbo engine with an 18.3 kWh battery for 56 miles (90 km) of WLTP electric range. Power is 150 kW (204 PS), and it starts at £35,170 in the UK. Australia now also gets an AWD version with a second, rear motor.

The Jaecoo 8 is a three-row, six- or seven-seat PHEV with three motors and AWD. It has a 34.46 kWh battery for 83 miles (134 km) of WLTP electric range, 315 kW (428 PS), and a 0-100 km/h time of 5.8 seconds. It starts at £45,500 in the UK.

The Omoda 9 is the brand’s flagship. It uses the same 34.46 kWh battery as the Jaecoo 8, rated at 90 miles (145 km) of WLTP electric range, with 449 PS and 700 Nm from an AWD setup. It does 0-100 km/h in 4.9 seconds and starts at £44,995 in the UK.

[IMG:6]

The Omoda 7 is a newer mid-size PHEV with 150 kW (204 PS), 56 miles (90 km) of electric range, and a UK starting price of £32,005.

It's sad to see Chinese EV makers pawning off their plug-in hybrids in overseas markets while the Chinese domestic market shifts decisively towards proper BEVs. The trade agreements of Canada, Europe, and everyone else should be "Sell us BEVs that reduce our greenhouse emissions and sales of dirty fossil fuel." Not half-steps.

Here’s how the lineup stacks up:

Chery also sells non-plug-in hybrid versions of several of these models, but those aren’t what the brand is pitching to Canadians as “electric SUVs.”

[IMG:7]

While I’m excited for Chinese EVs to hit the market, I’m not gonna lie: I’m not particularly excited by any of these. I’ll give them a shot. But on paper, this is pale in comparison to what other Chinese EVs have to offer.

queue.title: Think gas prices are too low? Don’t fret, Trump just raised them even higher
queue.text:
The Department of Transportation has finalized new fuel economy standards that will raise gas prices by 76 cents a gallon and fuel use by 44%, right as the world struggles with the effects of a war of choice that has
spiked energy prices globally
, reaching all-time highs in the US.

Update:
This article was originally published on September 2, when DoT said the change would be announced “soon.” The rule is now finalized, officially putting US on a path towards irrelevance for the US auto industry and much higher fuel costs for Americans.

Since the 1970s, the US government has had various rules that guide auto manufacturers to make and sell more efficient vehicles.

The main standards, Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE), were first implemented after the Arab oil embargo of the 1970s, and the ensuing energy crisis. The standards require manufacturers to maintain an average level of fuel efficiency across their fleet, or else they have to pay a fine for every noncompliant car they sell.

Prior to these standards, American cars were large and gas guzzling, with very little interest in efficiency. CAFE standards and other government regulations related to efficiency and clean air, both on the state and federal level, have made cars cleaner and more efficient as time has gone on.

The result of cleaner and more efficient vehicles is that it costs less to fuel them, costs less to breathe the dirty air they cause, and makes the environment that you depend on for everything good in your life more livable.

Overall, the policy has saved $5 trillion and stopped the import of 2 trillion gallons of gasoline, according to
a study released in 2020
. And that doesn’t even account for the environmental and health savings.

So, of course, republicans want to end all of that.

On Saturday, Sean Duffy, the
corrupt
former
reality TV contestant
posing as the current head of the Department of Transportation, said that this assault on Americans’ pocketbooks was “COMING MONDAY,” quoting a statement by Mr. Trump that falsely portrayed the changes as being a rollback of an
EV mandate that never existed
.

And today, the rule was
officially finalized
.

These changes in fuel economy standards aren’t a surprise – on his
very first day
, Duffy signed a memo promising to increase US fuel costs, reversing standards that were estimated to save Americans $23 billion. But his intent was to target
any
fuel economy standard whatsoever, wanting to eliminate anything that saves you money, as $23 billion wasn’t enough for him.

Over time, that intent has been refined and
officially proposed
as a reduction in 2031 target average fuel economy from 50.4mpg to 34.9mpg. The NHTSA says that in fact, these changes would raise fuel costs by $185 billion, and carbon emissions by 5%. These numbers do not take into account the higher health costs from more pollution (but the White House
literally says your life is worth nothing
, anyway).

Then it was
put up for public comment
, and the vast majority of the
68,294 comments
naturally opposed the plan to hike your fuel and health costs and make the environment less livable.

Doing some simple math, lowering fuel economy from 50.4 mpg to 34.9 mpg would raise the average fuel required to go the same distance by 44% – meaning that average total fuel costs will go up by
at least
44% if cars meet the new standards rather than the old ones.

Why “at least” 44%? Well, not only would this regulation mean that drivers have to buy more gasoline on average, but it also means that gasoline prices would go up even further as demand goes up.

You need look no further than
an analysis released by the Department of Energy
which said that gas prices will go up by 76 cents per gallon if republicans’ energy plans were to take effect. And before anyone claims partisanship – this report was signed off on by Chris Wright, the oil CEO
currently squatting in the DoE (who of course sees higher gas prices as a good thing, since it makes more money for his industry).

Mr. Trump falsely claims that this change will “lower prices,” but a report signed off on
by his own people
acknowledges that not only will prices go up, but that usage will increase – so you’ll be paying more per gallon

queue.title: BYD is overhauling its cheapest EV, and it’s bigger than expected
queue.text:
BYD
is giving its $10,000 EV a major overhaul. New images of the second-gen Seagull reveal a larger, more upscale design with a few surprise luxury features.

Sold as the Dolphin Surf in places like Europe and the UK, and as the Dolphin Mini in other global markets, the Seagull is BYD’s lowest-priced electric car.

BYD is known for its low-cost vehicles, but the Seagull is much cheaper than anything you can get your hands on in the US.

In China, it starts at just 69,900 yuan, or about $10,000. The most affordable in the US, on the other hand, is the 2026 Hyundai Venue, which you can buy for just over $20,000. Even in Europe, the Dolphin Surf starts at just €22,900.

The electric hatch is not only one of BYD’s most popular vehicles, but it’s also among the top-selling EVs in the world.

In the first half of 2026, the Seagull, along with the Dolphin Surf and Mini, ranked as the world’s sixth-best-selling EV. BYD sold
over 152,000 units
through June, according to data from
Cleantechnica
.

BYD is overhauling the electric hatch for its second generation to compete with the new wave of entry-level EVs hitting the market.

In a social media post on Wednesday, BYD offered a sneak peek at the interior, revealing a few surprises.

According to BYD, “Growing Up” means living up to expectations. The second-generation Seagull will feature an immersive cockpit with ambient lighting and power-adjustable front seats with massage functions. Although it didn’t reveal specifics, BYD said the rear seats are extra spacious with more legroom for passengers.

Inside, the second-gen Seagull adopts BYD’s new interior design. The setup includes a larger center infotainment screen, a two-spoke steering wheel, and a redesigned center console to create more space.

The new Seagull does not feature an instrument display. Instead, the larger center infotainment screen will display the information. BYD also added physical buttons below the center display.

BYD revealed the new Seagull will also include a “rare” 94L front trunk for its class, up to 1,380L of trunk space, and smart storage spaces.

Zhang Zhuo, general manager of BYD’s Ocean series, revealed the
first official images
of the new Seagull last week in a series of design sketches previewing the new interior and exterior.

[IMG:1]

Translated into English, one of the interior captions read: “Brand new layout” and “Space size expands together.”

BYD has yet to announce any official details, but Zhuo revealed at the Chengdu Auto Show last month that the second-gen model will be named the “Great Seagull” and will go on sale by the end of 2026.

We knew the second-gen Seagull would be a bigger variant, hence the “Great,” after the new variant appeared in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) regulatory filing in August.

According to the filing, the new Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase.

Compared to the current model, the second-gen Seagull is 425 mm longer with a 150 mm longer wheelbase. The current Seagull is only 3,780 mm long.

The filing also revealed it will use a more powerful 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from the 55 kW (75 hp) the current Seagull offers.

We’ve also seen spy images of the upgraded model testing in public with roof-mounted LiDAR, suggesting the second-gen Seagull will offer more advanced smart driving assistance capabilities, such as BYD’s God’s Eye B system.

A report from China’s
Autohome
on Monday revealed new exterior images of the second-generation Seagull EV.

The report also said the new Seagull will switch to a rear-mounted electric motor, replacing the front motor the current model uses. The change will open up space in the front trunk, or frunk.

BYD has yet to confirm details, but local reports suggest higher-priced variants may feature its latest Blade LFP Batteries 2.0 and 5-minute Flash Charging technology.

queue.title: Tesla (TSLA) Q3 2026 delivery estimates range from 422,000 to 482,000
queue.text:
Wall Street can’t agree on how many cars Tesla (TSLA) sold in Q3 2026. Estimates from major banks range from 421,758 to 482,000 deliveries ahead of Friday’s report.

That’s a 60,000-unit spread. And after the Street missed Tesla’s Q2 deliveries by 74,000 units, nobody has much credibility on this one.

Tesla reports Q3 production and deliveries on Friday, October 2. It hasn’t published its own company-compiled analyst consensus yet. For Q2, that figure came out six days before the report.

Here’s where the major firms stand as of today:

The median of those six is about 458,000. The Visible Alpha consensus sits between 449,000 and 454,000 depending on when you check it, while Bloomberg’s consensus is at 466,000.

Prediction markets are more bullish. Kalshi contracts currently put Q3 deliveries in the low-to-mid 470,000s, down from roughly 480,000 in mid-September. UBS analyst Joseph Spak also wrote that buy-side expectations have crept up to a 460,000 to 480,000 range.

The direction over the last two weeks is one-way. Goldman cut its estimate by 55,000 units on September 16, JPMorgan cut by 34,000 units today, and Cantor just came in with the lowest number on the Street.

The analysts all point to the same thing: a weak August in Tesla’s two biggest markets. Tesla’s US sales fell 26% year-over-year to about 40,816 units in the month, and its China retail sales dropped 12.4% to 50,047 units.

None of that is new if you’ve been following along.
Tesla’s China retail sales have been crashing even as exports surge
, and
EV sales are plunging in North America while Europe booms
.

Every single one of these estimates means a year-over-year decline. Tesla delivered a record 497,099 vehicles in Q3 2025, a quarter juiced by US buyers rushing to grab the $7,500 federal tax credit before it expired on September 30, 2025.

[IMG:1]

Even JPMorgan’s 482,000 would be down 3%. The median implies an 8% drop. Cantor’s number would be a 15% decline.

Sequentially, most estimates also point down from the
480,126 vehicles Tesla delivered in Q2
. Only JPMorgan expects growth.

But the Street has a bad recent track record here. Tesla’s company-compiled consensus for Q2 was
406,024 deliveries
. Tesla beat it by 74,000 units, and Kalshi traders landed almost exactly on the actual number.

It is a tough one to estimate. Normally, US should be significantly down year-over-year, but the war in the Middle East is a godsend, or rather Trump-send, for Tesla.

High gas prices could be almost fully compensating for the difference in demand from the end of the tax credit.

Tesla has been significantly down in China this quarter, but the last month is always the biggest, and Tesla has been offering discounts to bring demand back. A lot will depend on how successful those discounts will be.

Cathie's bear case for 2026 is 10 million cars sold at an ASP of $38k and gross margin of 50%.

Exports from China to other Asian, Pacific, and EU markets will help tremendously, but ultimately, I expect Tesla’s deliveries to be roughly flat to slightly down vs. Q3 last year.

Can you imagine where it would be if it wasn’t for Elon’s dumb moves to bet the house on autonomy? What if Tesla had a Model 2 (or E, or whatever) right now priced at $25,000-$30,000, in production in China, in the US, and Europe, based on the unboxed platform, which was the original plan.

Amid this gas price crisis, Tesla would be delivering almost twice as many vehicles, in my opinion.

queue.title: Tesla delays Roadster demo two weeks to October 15, blames weather
queue.text:
Tesla has officially pushed its Roadster demo from October 1 to October 15, blaming “severe conditions” in the forecast for central Texas.

It’s the latest in a long line of delays for the next-gen Roadster, and this one moves the event back two full weeks for what Tesla describes as a weather problem.

This morning, we
reported that Tesla warned invitees the October 1 Roadster demo could be rescheduled due to weather
. A few hours later, the company made it official in a
post on X
:

“We’ve been tracking the weather closely with local meteorologists, but given the severe conditions predicted & because this event can only be held outdoors, we’ve made the difficult decision to reschedule. New date is October 15.”

Tesla says “additional details” will follow. October 15 is also a Thursday, exactly two weeks after the original date.

The event is expected to take place at SpaceX’s rocket test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco. As we
reported in August
, the plan is to make the Roadster hover using a SpaceX-developed cold gas thruster package, with nobody in the car and spectators kept several hundred yards back.

To be fair to Tesla, the weather on October 1 does look bad. Open-Meteo forecast data for McGregor, updated Monday afternoon, now calls for an 82% chance of precipitation on Thursday, with thunderstorms, gusts around 30 mph, and more than 4 inches of rain.

But it doesn’t last. Friday still shows an 81% chance of rain, but with less than half an inch and gusts dropping to about 21 mph. By Saturday, it’s down to 53% with 13 mph gusts. From Sunday onward, the forecast is mostly dry, with no measurable rain from October 5 through October 7.

[IMG:1]

In other words, the storm passes within two or three days. Tesla picked a date two weeks out.

The Roadster has been delayed so many times that the list is hard to keep straight. Tesla unveiled the prototype in November 2017 with a promise of production in 2020. The “flying” demo was supposed to happen by the end of 2025, then
on April 1, 2026
, then late April, then “maybe in a month or so,” then
August
, then October 1.

Now it’s October 15. Production is still guided for “2027 or 2028.”

We’re not buying that this is only about the weather.

If the storm on Thursday were the only issue, Tesla would have pushed the event by a day or two. The forecast is dry by the weekend. Sure, rescheduling an event with invited guests takes some logistics, and maybe the site needs time to dry out after 4 inches of rain. But two weeks is a long buffer for a storm that’s gone by Saturday.

Guys, it's totally the weather and nothing else, for sure. If you haven't noticed, it's been raining and snowing and hailing in Waco for the past 7 years straight. The Roadster would've been shown years ago if not for that.

Bad news though: Musk's supercomputer forecasts bad weather in Waco for the next 50 years. How unfortunate.

We wouldn’t be surprised if Tesla is running into issues with the demo itself. This is a car that’s supposed to hover on SpaceX thrusters, operated remotely, in front of a crowd. Musk himself reportedly told staff it “will be hard to pull off and could go wrong.” A convenient storm buys time.

And honestly, that’s the frustrating part. Nobody who put down $50,000 or $250,000 for a Roadster asked for a hover stunt. We just want the Roadster Tesla unveiled nearly a decade ago: a fast electric sports car with a real price, real specs, and a real delivery date.

Will October 15 finally deliver that, or just another gimmick?

queue.title: EIA: 83 GW of renewables and storage coming in 12 months as fossil fuel capacity to fall
queue.text:
Renewables and battery storage are projected to add about 82.7 gigawatts (GW) of new generating capacity in the US in the next 12 months, while total fossil fuel and nuclear power capacity will fall by more than 1.4 GW, according to new data released by the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), and reviewed by the SUN DAY Campaign.

According to the EIA’s latest “Electric Power Monthly” report (with data through July 31, 2026), renewably generated electricity during the first seven months of 2026 was 10.7% greater than in the same period of 2025. The growth was led by utility-scale solar (up 22.0%), small-scale solar (up 12.6%), hydropower (up 9.0%), and wind (up 5.9%).

By comparison, the electrical output of US natural gas and nuclear power plants grew much more slowly – by just 1.8% and 1.5%, respectively. Electricity produced by US coal facilities fell by 10.2%.

The combination of wind and solar, including small-scale solar, accounted for 21.6% of US electricity production. Further, they produced 49% more electricity than the US’s coal plants and 26% more than its nuclear reactors.

In July, for the second month in a row, solar-generated electricity was the leading renewable energy source. In fact, solar produced almost as much electricity as wind and hydropower combined.

The mix of all renewables, including biomass and geothermal, accounted for over 29.0% of total US electrical generation – up from 26.8% year over year.

During the first 18 months of the second Trump administration (between February 1, 2025, and July 31, 2026), the installed capacity of utility-scale solar increased by 32.7% (41,051.6 megawatts (MW)) while that of small-scale solar and wind grew by 17.0% (9,112.4 MW) and 8.0% (12,195.4 MW, including 800 MW of offshore wind), respectively.

The combined capacity of all renewable energy sources, including hydropower, biomass, and geothermal, expanded by 14.6% (62,092.0 MW).

In addition, utility-scale battery energy storage capacity doubled, adding 26,629.5 MW.

Thus, renewables plus battery storage have grown by over 88,700 MW.

By comparison, coal capacity fell by 2.4% (-4,131.8 MW) as nuclear power added just 0.8% (800.6 MW). Natural gas capacity rose by 1.5% (7,561.5 MW). The combined generating capacity of all fossil fuels, including oil and “other” gases, plus nuclear power, rose by a mere 0.3% (2,641.0 MW).

[IMG:1]

EIA projects that over the next 12 months (through July 31, 2027), utility-scale solar will add 43,558.0 MW while wind will grow by 9,481.8 MW (including 3,355.0 MW of offshore wind). The mix of other renewables (i.e., hydropower, biomass, and geothermal) will add 193.6 MW.

EIA also projects battery energy storage will add another 23,428.9 MW by August 1, 2027.

EIA does not provide a forecast for the next 12 months of small-scale solar capacity growth, but the SUN DAY Campaign forecasts it will equal or exceed the roughly 6,000 MW added on average over the past five years.

Thus, the combination of utility-scale renewable energy sources and battery energy storage could provide 76,662.3 MW of new clean energy capacity by mid-summer 2027. With the inclusion of small-scale solar, that figure could rise to about 82,700 MW.

For the same period, EIA projects no new nuclear generating capacity and a net decline of 1,452.7 MW in fossil fuel capacity.

Solar, wind and battery are the cheapest form of energy a utility can install. Also, unlike oil or natural gas, the price of electricity is not traded globally so world events don't influence the price. Solar and wind are the best choice for national energy independence.

“Over the last 18 months, the Trump Administration has used every conceivable trick to delay, hinder, or cancel new clean energy projects,” noted the SUN DAY Campaign’s executive director, Ken Bossong. “Yet, while fossil fuels and nuclear power have added just 2.6 GW of net new capacity, renewables and battery storage have grown by 88.7 GW. Clearly, the White House has bet on the wrong horse.”

queue.title: New York considering 20+ new e-bike laws including outlawing Class 3 electric bikes
queue.text:
New York City lawmakers are preparing this week to consider a sweeping new package of micromobility legislation, with more than 20 bills aimed at e-bikes, electric scooters, mopeds, delivery apps, and enforcement.

Some of the proposals
look like fairly reasonable attempts to deal with actual problems surrounding illegal or modified electric bikes. Others go considerably further, including several bills that would effectively eliminate an entire category of legal e-bikes from New York City.

According to
Gothamist
, the New York City Council’s Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure is set to meet Wednesday to discuss the collection of bills, which range from increased enforcement against illegal vehicles to new requirements for food delivery platforms.

For a bit of background,
New York legalized e-bikes statewide in 2020
and created three categories. Class 1 e-bikes use pedal assist up to 20 mph (32 km/h), Class 2 e-bikes can also use a throttle up to 20 mph (32 km/h), and Class 3 e-bikes can provide motor assistance up to 25 mph (40 km/h). Riders must be at least 16 years old, but legal e-bikes don’t require a driver’s license or vehicle registration.

Several of the proposed bills focus on devices that already fall outside those definitions.

One would establish a program allowing the NYPD and New York City Department of Transportation to use a dynamometer to test suspected illegal micromobility vehicles for their motor power and maximum assisted speed. That could give police an objective way of determining whether a bike has been modified or is simply an electric motorcycle masquerading as an e-bike.

There are also proposals aimed at delivery companies.

One would require delivery apps to verify that mopeds used by workers are properly registered, while another would require the companies to submit annual safety reports and plans.

Councilmember Gale Brewer has introduced a bill that would require food delivery apps to carry liability insurance covering crashes involving workers making deliveries or available to make deliveries.

Those measures could have an especially large impact considering the Workers Justice Project estimates around 80,000 e-bike delivery workers operate in New York City.

But then we get to the Class 3 proposals.

Three bills would specifically target Class 3 e-bikes, the fastest class of e-bikes, which are currently legal under New York’s e-bike framework.

Councilmember Crystal Hudson has introduced legislation that would prohibit shops from selling or renting Class 3 e-bikes. A first violation wouldn’t result in a fine, but subsequent violations could bring penalties of up to $2,000.

A separate Hudson bill would go considerably further by prohibiting people from riding Class 3 e-bikes on streets, in parks, or in other public spaces.

[IMG:1]

And Transportation Committee Chair Shaun Abreu has proposed creating a trade-in program allowing owners of Class 3 and other ineligible e-bikes to exchange them for a Class 1 or Class 2 e-bike, or receive a voucher toward purchasing one.

That last proposal would presumably help soften the impact if Class 3 bikes were ultimately prohibited, but it also highlights just how significant a change the city is considering.

There is an important distinction between cracking down on illegally modified e-bikes and simply making currently legal e-bikes illegal.

New York already draws a regulatory line at 25 mph (40 km/h) for Class 3 e-bikes – an unfortuantley arbitrary figure compared to the commonly accepted 28 mph (45 km/h) standard in the vast majority of the US, but one that has so far worked. In theory, if riders are operating devices that exceed the legal limits, enforcement tools such as dynamometer testing could help authorities identify those vehicles without sweeping legal e-bikes into the same category. It’s already
employed in Europe
to good effect.

I don't think that it's exactly controversial to insist that a vehicle, used in commerce, be licensed and the driver/rider be insured.

NYC might also reasonably split the baby and simply ban Class 3 bikes from Manhattan.

The proposed Class 3 ban takes a different approach by moving that line downward and removing a category of e-bike that New York currently permits.

It also comes amid a broader push to reduce e-bike speeds in New York City. Last year, the city ordered Citi Bike to reduce the top assisted speed of its gray electric bikes from 18 mph (30 km/h) to 15 mph (25 km/h).

Whether New York City ultimately adopts any of these proposals remains to be seen. Wednesday’s committee meeting is part of the legislative process, and New Yorkers have been invited to testify either in person or remotely.

But with more than 20 micromobility bills arriving at once, the debate is becoming less about whether New York should regulate e-bikes and more about where exactly lawmakers should draw the line between addressing illegal vehicles and placing new restrictions on the legal ones already being used across the city.

queue.text:
Lexus
confirmed the 2027 TZ will go on sale later this year with prices starting under $65,000. The electric SUV will offer up to 315 miles of range on a single charge.

While the Toyota Highlander BEV and Subaru Getaway
won’t arrive until 2027
as 2028 model-year vehicles now, Lexus will beat both with its first three-row electric SUV.

Lexus said the TZ will go on sale later this year as a 2027 model year. It will be available in three trims, starting at $64,050. The prices include a $1,550 delivery fee.

Based on the same platform as the electric Highlander, the Lexus TZ will be offered with two battery packs: 76.96 kWh and 95.82 kWh. The former provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 253 miles, while the latter gets up to 315 miles of range, slightly less than Lexus’ 320-mile estimate.

While it offers a bit less range, all TZ models come standard with an “evolved” version of its DIRECT4 AWD system.

The dual-motor AWD setup delivers a combined 308 horsepower, considerably less than the estimated 402 horsepower Lexus initially said.

Although it shares the same underpinnings as the Highlander BEV and Subaru Getaway, Lexus promises the TZ will look and feel like a Lexus, with fine-tuned suspension, dynamic rear steering, and reinforced body structure.

Inside, the three-row electric SUV features the latest Lexus Interface multimedia system. The setup includes customizable widgets, an improved Voice Assistant, and full-screen navigation on the digital cluster.

[IMG:1]

It also includes new functions to help you find and navigate to EV charging stations, including EV Routing and EV Range Map.

The 2027 Lexus TZ is 200.8″ long, 78.3″ wide, and 67.1″ tall, with a 120.1″ wheelbase, or about the same size as the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and the Volvo EX90.

Lexus said the electric SUV can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 35 minutes at up to 150 kW. It also includes an NACS charge port so you can access Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter.

Pretty slow charging speed for a "luxury EV".

The base 2027 Lexus TZ 450e Premium AWD will be available later this year, starting at $64,050 with up to 253 miles of range.

The Touring and Luxury models will go on sale in early 2027, starting at $72,050 and $80,550, respectively. Both use the larger 95.82 kWh battery, but the Touring model offers up to 315 miles of range, while the top-spec Luxury trim gets 279 miles.

queue.title: US clean energy jobs fell for the first time since the pandemic
queue.text:
The US lost 36,949 clean energy jobs in 2025, ending four straight years of growth. That’s the direct impact of the Trump administration and the Republican-controlled Congress rolling back federal support for clean energy and EVs, which led companies to cancel or scale back projects.

That’s according to
new findings from E2
, which analyzed employment data from the US Department of Energy. Clean energy employment fell to 3.52 million, the first annual decline since the pandemic. The jobs lost in 2025 erased nearly 40% of the gains made in 2024.

The losses reached 35 states. California shed nearly 21,000 clean energy jobs, the most of any state, while Florida gained about 3,800. Energy efficiency, renewable energy, and EVs all lost jobs. Battery storage and grid work, along with biofuels, posted small gains.

E2 connects the downturn to the federal policy reversal and the resulting rise in project cancellations. Its
project tracker
recorded 142 clean energy manufacturing, generation, and storage projects canceled or downsized in 2025. The employment figures show the extent of the decline, but don’t establish how many of those jobs were lost due to a particular policy change.

Clean energy wasn’t the only sector losing workers. The broader US energy industry shed an estimated 86,000 jobs in 2025, according to the DOE data cited by E2. Clean energy accounted for roughly 43% of that decline, but it remains the largest part of the energy workforce, employing more than 3.5 million people. Compare that to oil and gas companies, which employ 958,000 workers; coal companies, with 125,000 employees; and nuclear companies, with 70,000 workers.

queue.title: Tesla patents ‘Electric Fan Car’ with 4 ducted fans ahead of Roadster reveal
queue.text:
Tesla was just granted a patent for an “Electric Fan Car,” a system that uses four electric ducted fans in the rear diffuser to suck the car down to the road at any speed. The car in the drawings is a Model S, which Tesla stopped building in April.

It’s Tesla’s second fan car patent in just over a year, and it arrives two weeks before the company’s latest attempt at a Roadster demo.

The USPTO granted
US 12,746,987 B1
today. Tesla filed it in January 2024, but it goes back to a provisional application from January 17, 2023. Eight inventors are listed, and all but one are based in the Los Angeles area, where Tesla has its design studio in Hawthorne.

The idea is simple. An inlet on the underbody, between the rear wheels, feeds a duct that sweeps up to a wide outlet in the rear diffuser. Four axial fans sit side by side in that outlet, split by three vertical strakes. When they spin up, they evacuate the air under the floor and exhaust it through the rear.

That creates what Tesla calls a “suction region” under the floor. A vacuum. The rear end also gets a raked plate that acts as a second diffuser.

Tesla’s pitch is about speed independence. The filing notes that passive diffusers limit downforce at low speed and “often results in an excessive load at a high speed.” The fans, according to Tesla, “can produce a downforce independent of the vehicle velocity,” which helps with braking stability and cornering speed.

There’s one clever detail. A second version adds two smaller side inlets behind the main one, because Tesla says the central inlet tends to pull air forward from behind the car instead of from under the floor. That backwash adds no downforce, and Tesla says the fans end up “wasting power” on it.

Power comes from the same high-voltage pack that drives the wheels, so there’s no separate motor or battery for the fans, and they’re tied into the car’s control system. The driver can switch them on with a button, or the car can do it automatically at certain speeds.

You can’t miss the Model S in these drawings. The fastback roofline, taillights, lip spoiler and door handles are all there.

In early 2023, when Tesla filed the provisional, that made sense. The Model S Plaid was Tesla’s performance flagship, and a fan-assisted track version would have been a fun halo. But
Tesla ended Model S and Model X production
in April after 14 years, and it’s turning the Fremont line over to Optimus. So that’s not happening.

Which leaves the Roadster, the only performance car Tesla still has in the pipeline. Last week, we reported on
a Tesla patent for a hidden active rear wing
good for up to 700 kg of downforce, drawn on a car that looks just like the new Roadster. And in August 2025, Tesla got
another fan car patent
using underbody fans and deployable skirts. Fans plus an active wing is a full track aero package, and the Roadster is the only car left to put it on.

[IMG:1]

None of this is new. Chaparral raced the 2J in 1970 with two fans driven by a separate snowmobile engine. Brabham’s BT46B won the 1978 Swedish Grand Prix with Niki Lauda and was withdrawn right after. Gordon Murray put a 400 mm fan on the back of the T.50 road car.

And on the electric side, McMurtry has been doing it for years. Its Spéirling
smashed the all-time Goodwood hill climb record in June 2022
, about seven months before Tesla filed its provisional. It makes 2,000 kg of downforce at a standstill, has
driven upside down
, and McMurtry
started production of the $1.36 million Spéirling PURE
earlier this year. Its fans also run off the main battery.

Tesla’s main twist is that its design doesn’t need skirts sealing the car to the ground. The filing says the fans can work “without use of additional elements below the vehicle,” and packages them into a normal-looking diffuser.

It’s a neat patent, but electric fan cars exist; they’re on sale, and McMurtry got there first by a wide margin. Putting the fans in the diffuser without skirts is a packaging choice. And without skirts, it’s hard to see Tesla getting anywhere near the 2,000 kg the Spéirling makes.

"Power comes from the same high-voltage pack that drives the wheels, so there’s no separate motor or battery for the fan"

This seems weird. Obviously makes sense to have the fans running off the main power system, but no separate motor would mean some kind of weird transmission thingy to make the fans spin. Quite possible that the designers hadn't bothered to work out the details, so the patent just ignored that part to avoid limiting coverage to one particular setup.

(If the fans are going to do what the patent apparently says they do, each one will need its own motor and controller, and a bunch of sensors to match fan air draw to vehicle speed so that the downforce actually does stay under control.)

The Model S drawings say more than the claims do. Somebody at Tesla was clearly working on a track-focused Model S in 2023. That car is dead, and the idea has nowhere to go but the Roadster. Between this, last year’s skirted fan patent, and last week’s 700 kg wing, Tesla has built up a real track aero toolbox. That’s a lot more useful than making a car hover on SpaceX thrusters.

But patents aren’t products, and Tesla patents plenty of things that never ship. The Roadster was unveiled in 2017, promised for 2020, and is now
slated for “2027 or 2028” with a demo pushed to October 15
. If it finally shows up with fans in the back, great. We’d take that over a hover stunt any day.

Will we see fans on October 15, or just thrusters?

queue.title: Hyundai is launching two new EVs, the IONIQ 4 and IONIQ 7
queue.text:
Hyundai
is preparing to introduce two new electric SUVs, the IONIQ 4 and IONIQ 7, filling two key gaps in its EV lineup.

The IONIQ 5 is about the size of the Tesla Model Y, while the IONIQ 9 offers three rows of seating, but what if you wanted something in between?

Hyundai is launching two new electric SUVs as it expands into new segments. One will sit below the IONIQ 5, and the other between the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

The IONIQ 7 is slightly bigger than the IONIQ 5 and aimed more at families, offering more interior space. The IONIQ 4, on the other hand, is a B-segment SUV that will offer an option between the
recently launched IONIQ 3
and the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai has yet to confirm specifics, but Chris McKinnon, Hyundai Europe’s VP of product, told
Auto Express
to “watch this space” and to keep an eye out for more information on the upcoming B-segment SUV.

When asked if it will be similar to the Kia EV3, McKinnon said: “I really can’t answer that question, to be honest,” but added that the market was “important” for the Hyundai brand.

Like the EV3, the Hyundai IONIQ 4 is expected to feature a boxier, more SUV-like design than the IONIQ 3 and IONIQ 5.

Inside, the electric SUV will feature Hyundai’s new interior design, like the IONIQ 3. It’s also expected to have Hyundai’s next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.

We will learn more about the IONIQ 4 soon, but it’s expected to be available with similar battery pack options: 42 kWh and 61 kWh. The former provides up to 214 miles (344 km) of WLTP range. The latter gets up to 308 miles (497 km).

[IMG:1]

While the Kona Electric is still currently available in the UK, it is expected to be discontinued and replaced by the new IONIQ 4.

When it arrives, the Hyundai IONIQ 4 will likely start at around £25,000 ($33,000), or slightly more than the IONIQ 3.

The IONIQ 7 will fill the gap between the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 with two- or three-row seating options. It will be closer in size and price to
the IONIQ 5
, but with a boxier, SUV-like look. It will be available with dual- and single-motor powertrains.

An Ioniq "7" with a small, fold-away or removeable third row would be a great option. The 9 is BIG, and my family wouldn't need the third row except for when we're visiting family and want to go to dinner or a day-trip in one car.

No other details have been confirmed, but the IONIQ 7 is expected to offer a WLTP range of at least 400 miles and fast charging with an 800V architecture.

It will also be equipped with Hyundai Pleos and is expected to start at around £45,000 to £50,000 ($60,000 to $66,000) in the UK.

Will Hyundai bring either to the US? Don’t get your hopes up. Although Hyundai has not officially announced either model, the IONIQ 4 and IONIQ 7 are likely designed for the European market. We should learn more soon, with both set to launch in the next 12 to 18 months.

queue.title: Two Silverado EVs and a 150 kWh battery powered this entire concert tour
queue.text:
A five-stop concert tour in Quebec ran entirely on two Chevrolet Silverado EVs and a 150 kWh mobile power plant this summer. No diesel generator, and no hookup to the grid.

I went to the final show, held in a grocery store parking lot in Montreal’s Saint-Henri neighborhood, and everything from the speakers to the stage lights to the kitchen was running off batteries.

A free tour powered by EV batteries

The tour, called “Le goût du paysage” (roughly “a taste of the landscape”), was put together by Papillons . That’s the Quebec company behind the RechargÉco fast-charging network, which it operates across Quebec and New Brunswick.

[IMG:1]

The idea was simple: bring Québécois artists Émile Proulx-Cloutier and Dumas, along with chef Oli cooking free corn dishes made with regional ingredients, to scenic spots across the province. Admission was free.

It ran from August 15 to 22 with stops in Trois-Pistoles, the Vallée Bras-du-Nord in Saint-Raymond, Parc Éco-Laurentides in Mont-Blanc, and Île-aux-Castors in Berthierville (that one sold out). The tour wrapped up with both artists on stage in the IGA parking lot in Saint-Henri.

Papillons billed the whole production as “100%” powered by EV batteries, with “zero emissions from start to finish.” Based on what I saw on site, that’s accurate.

[IMG:2]

Two pickups running the stage

The two Silverado EVs handled the stage: the sound system, the lighting, and the site lights once the sun went down. In Saint-Henri, I could follow the cable straight out of the power outlet in one truck’s bed to the stage.

It’s a good job for the truck. The Silverado EV can be had with up to a 205 kWh battery pack, one of the biggest you can buy in a consumer vehicle, and GM rates its onboard power at 7.2 kW to 10.2 kW depending on the trim. We’ve already seen GM run an entire mansion off a Silverado EV when it launched its GM Energy products, and the 2026 Silverado EV only pushed range further.

For comparison, Ford’s F-150 Lightning tops out at 9.6 kW of onboard power. And Tesla only just added 2.4 kW of vehicle-to-load to the Model Y Premium , and you need an $80 adapter for it.

[IMG:3]

The kitchen ran on a 150 kWh mobile power plant

The kitchen is the hard part. Cooking equipment pulls a lot of power, and it runs for hours.

For that, Papillons used a trailer-mounted mobile power plant with 150 kWh of energy capacity. It powered chef Oli’s kitchen at every stop.

Full disclosure: my company, Ixian , was involved in this project. We helped Papillons engineer the mobile power plant. Papillons isn’t ready to share more details about the system just yet, so I’ll leave it at that for now, but you can reach out to them if you are interested in such a product.

At the Saint-Henri stop, the trailer was parked right next to the kitchen tent, feeding full-size electric ranges topped with giant stockpots.

[IMG:4]

Why bother with batteries in the city?

The show I attended was in the middle of Montreal. There’s power everywhere in Saint-Henri: the grocery store, the buildings around the lot, the streetlights.

But having power nearby and being allowed to use it are two different things. Getting a temporary connection for an event usually means dealing with the utility or the property owner, hiring an electrician, and paying for all of it, often for a single evening. Plenty of organizers skip the headache and rent a diesel generator instead.

[IMG:5]

With batteries, you roll in, plug in, and you’re done. And on a stage where people are there for quiet acoustic songs, the lack of a rumbling generator behind the crowd matters.

But the real advantage showed up at the other four stops. A riverside island in Berthierville, a valley in Saint-Raymond, a park in the Laurentians. There’s no grid access at those spots, period. Normally, that’s where the diesel generators come out, if the show happens at all.

And the energy itself is about as clean as it gets. The trucks and the power plant recharge on Quebec’s grid, which Hydro-Québec says is over 99% renewable, mostly hydro.

[IMG:6]

I can think of quite a few people that would fall in love with an EV if they were able to get one in their budget that has the capability to provide power for their home.  They have quite a few power outages in their area and use generators a lot, but having a car as backup with be a game changer for them.  Interestingly enough, some much more affordable Chinese EVs mostly have these features and coming to Canada very soon.

Events are a great fit for mobile power supply. Festivals, outdoor concerts, film shoots, and construction sites burn a lot of diesel in rented generators, and they do it right next to people. A big battery on wheels does the same job silently, with no fumes, and it can be recharged at a charging station between stops. It helps that Papillons runs a fast-charging network.

The limit right now is output. Even the Silverado EV caps out around 10 kW per truck, which is plenty for sound and lights but not enough for everything.

[IMG:7]

But the concept works. I saw it work. It’s a great use case example for bidirectional charging, which I think is going to become an increasingly important part of the EV revolution.

queue.title: Hyundai starts selling electric Ioniq V for under $15,000, but you can’t have it
queue.text:
Hyundai has officially launched the Ioniq V in China, starting for a limited time at under $15,000 – a budget EV, but without budget specs. The Chinese rollout comes ahead of a planned global launch.

But, as usual, if you’re reading this from America, you can’t have it.

The Ioniq V debuted just
five months ago at the Beijing Auto Show
(just weeks after its
concept reveal
), with a shockingly angular design, looking like a low-polygon version of the new Toyota Prius.

It’s the beginning salvo in Hyundai’s 20-model planned entry into the crowded Chinese EV market, and the rest of the vehicles are expected to use similar design language.

Now, after doing a
soft-launch at the Chengdu Auto Show
wherein it started taking pre-orders, Hyundai has officially launched the vehicle, so we finally get all the information about its final specs.

When pre-sales started, Hyundai originally quoted a price of 119,900 yuan. But in China, cars quite commonly get released at a lower price than they’re announced at, and it looks like the Ioniq V will be no different, as it was announced today with a 109,900 yuan base price. Four other trims are available, with price points arranged thusly:

The 540 trims have a 53.5kWh LFP battery, 140kW (188hp) motor and a WLTP range of 443km (275mi). The 650 trims have a 66.8kWh LFP battery, 168kw (225hp) motor and WLTP range of 533km (331mi). CLTC ranges are higher, and both CLTC and WLTP ranges are more lenient than EPA, so consider all those range numbers somewhat inflated. Both batteries are supplied by CATL, the world’s largest automotive battery supplier.

But wait, there’s more!
In fact, the Ioniq V is available with a limited-time discount of 8,000-10,000 yuan, meaning you can in fact get the base model for just 99,900 yuan, which is just under $15,000. They’re also throwing in some additional warranty coverage on the introductory offer, including a battery degradation warranty (which shouldn’t matter, as LFP batteries are incredibly durable).

China truly loves to surprise and delight on prices.

While the Ioniq V looks like a blocky Toyota Prius, it’s quite a chunk longer – 192.9in (4,900mm), as compared to the Prius’ 181.1in (4,600mm). It’s also about 4 inches taller and wider (57.9in/1,470mm and 74.4in/1,890mm).

On the interior, the cockpit is centered around a massive 27-inch screen (Hyundai says its a 4K screen, but we’re not sure what that refers to – because 4K is typically 3840×2160, and that screen is certainly not that resolution) and uses two Chinese AI models, from Baidu and ByteDance.

For the driver, it comes equipped with a heads-up display it calls Cyber Eye, and includes a driver assistance system developed alongside Momenta, a Chinese ADAS company which supplies several brands.

The one spec-related question we had when we first heard about the Ioniq V was how quickly it would charge, and… we still can’t find an answer to that. We’ve reached out to Hyundai to see if we can get that information, and will update this when we hear back.

[IMG:1]

The car is built around Hyundai’s E-GMP platform, with 800V charging. This system underpins some of the
fastest charging cars in the US
.

But in China, EV charging is on another level entirely, with
1.5 megawatt charging stations
being deployed and
2.2 MW stations announced
, as cars
compete to save seconds, not minutes
off their charging time.

So Hyundai might have to up its game to compete in the Chinese market… or it can convince customers that a couple more minutes of charge time isn’t that big a deal.

Hyundai has suggested a future EREV version will come out, but given
EV sales are up and everything with an ICE engine is down
in China, we expect the BEV version to be the most popular.

While pre-orders are open in China, they’re not open anywhere else… yet. Hyundai acknowledges that China is at the forefront of global mobility, and thinks its entry into the country’s EV market will help it succeed globally.

I like the look of it, but I am kind of over the Bladerunner futuristic aggressive look of some vehicles. I like Rivian because they are more friendly looking, warm, balanced.

Seems like a good option for many though.

Which means it does want to offer the Ioniq V to worldwide markets, but it doesn’t have a timeline for that yet.

We’d imagine it’s very likely that the model will be sold Australia, where
EV sales are booming
and where Hyundai started selling the Elexio this year. We’re hoping it goes further, to rest-of-world markets, Europe and
possibly even Canada
.

But without a
change in policy
, the US is likely to be deprived of the
hottest
and
latest
tech
, not getting access to affordably-priced new vehicles that help
clean the air
and reduce both
energy costs
and
global conflict
, once again.

queue.title: Tesla (TSLA) wins SEC OK to auto-vote retail shares with board ahead of SpaceX merger
queue.text:
Tesla (TSLA) got the SEC’s blessing today to let retail shareholders sign up for a standing instruction that automatically votes their shares the way Tesla’s board recommends, at every meeting, until they cancel it.

The timing is hard to ignore. Tesla still hasn’t scheduled its 2026 annual meeting, and Elon Musk keeps teasing a SpaceX merger that could hand him a big chunk of his $1 trillion pay package without hitting a single operational goal.

Tesla’s general counsel Brandon Ehrhart and Sullivan & Cromwell sent the SEC’s Office of Mergers and Acquisitions a
no-action request
dated September 29. The SEC
signed off the same day
. A footnote in Tesla’s letter explains the quick turnaround: it followed “months-long” discussions with SEC staff.

Tesla calls it an “Issuer Voluntary Retail Voting Program.” Retail investors opt in, and from then on their votes are submitted “based on the recommendation of the company’s board of directors.” That’s the only instruction on the menu. There’s no option to vote against the board or to follow any other policy.

Participants pick one of two scopes: every matter, or every matter except contested director elections and mergers, acquisitions, or divestitures that require a shareholder vote. Under the first option, a retail holder’s shares would back the board on a merger automatically.

The votes are cast as soon as Tesla files its definitive proxy with the SEC, which is before shareholders even receive the proxy statement. Participants can still override any proposal or opt out for free, and they get a reminder at least once a year.

Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev
celebrated the approval on X
, saying Robinhood was “proud to work with the outstanding team at Tesla to help make this happen” and calling it “a voting program that empowers retail investors.” Tesla’s letter describes broker-run “Hubs” where investors could enroll in every participating company’s program in one go.

Tesla isn’t the first. ExxonMobil got similar relief in September 2025, and Tesla says more than 100,000 Exxon shareholders had enrolled by March. Goldman Sachs got its own letter yesterday. But Tesla wrote its request as a “framework,” and the SEC agreed the relief applies to any company that runs the program the same way.

Tesla’s pitch is that retail investors are underrepresented. It cites Broadridge data showing retail investors voted only 28% of their shares in the 2025 proxy season, compared to 76.6% for institutions. It also says it spent more than $2 million on proxy solicitors alone to get retail votes out at its last two annual meetings.

Those retail votes are the ones that decide close calls at Tesla. Last year, proxy advisers ISS and Glass Lewis told institutions to vote against Musk’s new pay package, and it
passed anyway
on the back of retail support.

The xAI vote at that same meeting is the better example. Shareholders put forward a proposal for Tesla to invest in Musk’s AI startup, and the board made no recommendation. It got about 1.06 billion votes for and 916 million against, but more than 473 million shares abstained. Tesla counts abstentions as votes against, so it failed.

Tesla
invested $2 billion in xAI anyway
in January. A few weeks later, SpaceX took over xAI, and Tesla’s stake turned into SpaceX stock.

And Tesla’s new letter doesn’t say what a standing instruction does when the board declines to make a recommendation, like it did on xAI.

Tesla’s last annual meeting was November 6, 2025. In an amended 10-K filed on April 30, Tesla said its board “has not yet established the date of the 2026 annual meeting of shareholders” and that the proxy would come late. Five months later, there’s still no proxy on EDGAR.

This isn’t new. Tesla also pushed its 2025 meeting to November and only set a date after shareholders publicly pressed the board over the delay.

[IMG:1]

Under Texas law, where Tesla reincorporated in 2024, a shareholder can ask a court to order a meeting once 13 months pass without one. For Tesla, that’s early December.

Musk has been hinting at a Tesla-SpaceX merger for months. On Tesla’s
Q2 earnings call in July
, he said the companies have “more and more overlap,” but “we can’t talk about combining companies and that kind of thing on a call.” A week later, the WSJ reported that Tesla was
weighing a sale of its China business
to clear the way for a deal.

SpaceX, which went public in June, is now worth about $2 trillion. Tesla was worth about $1.47 trillion last week. Musk owns about 20% of Tesla, but he controls over 80% of the voting power at SpaceX.

Now look at the change-in-control clause in Musk’s
2025 CEO Performance Award
. The award is 12 tranches of 35,311,992 shares each. Normally, each tranche needs a market cap milestone, starting at $2 trillion, plus an operational goal like 20 million vehicles, 1 million Optimus robots, or 1 million robotaxis in commercial operation.

In a change in control, the operational goals are dropped. Tesla measures market cap solely at the greater of the last closing price or the per-share price paid in the deal, with no six-month average required. Any tranche that hits its mark vests right away.

As we
explained in May
, that means a SpaceX takeover of Tesla at a price that values Tesla at $2 trillion would earn Musk his first tranche without Tesla delivering a single robotaxi. With roughly 3.95 billion Tesla shares outstanding, that’s about $506 per share, or around a 36% premium to last week’s price.

Musk would be on both sides of that price negotiation. And whatever deal comes out of it would need a shareholder vote, where a growing pool of retail shares could already be committed to whatever the board recommends.

The problem Tesla says it’s solving is real. Retail investors don’t vote, and that’s a problem for any company with as many small shareholders as Tesla.

But look at the fix. It’s a one-way switch. You can pre-commit your shares to the board, but you can’t pre-commit them against the board or hand them to an independent policy. If Tesla really wanted to make retail voting easier, it would offer both. It doesn’t.

If the problem is that individual shareholders are underrepresented because they don't vote, I don't understand how the solution is for the top people to vote for them.

And that board isn’t independent in any sense that matters here. It pushed the $1 trillion pay package through over the objections of both major proxy advisers, and it approved the xAI investment after shareholders turned it down.

So Tesla now has the SEC’s green light to lock in retail votes, an annual meeting it hasn’t scheduled, and a CEO hinting at a merger that would pay him on market cap alone. We can’t say for sure that these are connected. But Tesla is going to have to answer that question, and it should do it before shareholders are asked to vote on a deal with SpaceX.
